title: India's Banks Are the Healthiest in a Generation — and the RBI's New Stability Report Explains Why Investors Should Care
excerpt: The June 2026 Financial Stability Report shows bank bad loans below 2%, credit growth at 14.5%, and stress-tested resilience — but also flags risks from state government debt and global AI-bubble fragilities that NRI investors should watch.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India released its June 2026 Financial Stability Report on Tuesday, and the headline verdict is unambiguous: India's banking system is the healthiest it has been in a generation. But tucked inside the optimism are a set of emerging risks — from ballooning state government debt to global AI-bubble fragilities — that deserve more attention than they're getting.

## The Good News: Bad Loans at Historic Lows

Indian banks' combined gross non-performing asset (NPA) ratio stood at just **1.8 percent** at the end of March 2026. The RBI projects it will inch up only marginally, to 1.9 percent, by March 2028 under a baseline scenario. Anything below 2 percent is considered exceptionally healthy by global standards — and a far cry from the dark days of 2017-2018, when gross NPAs exceeded 11 percent and the entire banking system teetered under the weight of bad corporate loans.

Credit growth, meanwhile, accelerated to **14.5 percent** in fiscal year 2026, up from 11 percent the year before. State-owned banks, long the weakest link in the system, have been growing faster than their private sector peers — a reversal that would have seemed unlikely even three years ago. Bank profitability remains robust, supported by stable net interest margins, expanding loan books, and growing fee income.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra, in his foreword to the report, noted that "the Indian economy and the financial system have demonstrated remarkable resilience despite facing external shocks of significant magnitude" — a diplomatic reference to the US-Iran conflict that sent oil prices to $126 per barrel in April before they retreated to the current $73 range.

## Stress Tests: The System Can Take a Hit

The RBI's macro stress tests examined what would happen to banks under severe adverse scenarios — a sharp growth slowdown, spiking inflation, and a credit freeze. Even under the worst-case scenario, gross NPAs would rise to 3.8-4.1 percent by March 2028 — uncomfortable, but nowhere close to systemic. The report confirms that non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset management firms, clearing corporations, and insurance companies all passed their respective resilience tests.



> **"Foreign portfolio investors bought a record $3 billion in Indian government bonds in June alone — attracted by newly removed capital gains and withholding taxes."**


For NRI investors with exposure to Indian bank stocks — whether through HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, SBI, or Kotak Mahindra — the stress-test results provide a quantified reassurance that goes beyond management commentary. These are the RBI's own models, using data that banks can't spin.

## The Risks Beneath the Surface

The report isn't all sunshine. Two domestic risks stand out.

**First, banks are loading up on state government securities.** The share of commercial bank holdings in state government bonds has been rising sharply, driven by their higher yields compared with central government paper. At 36.1 percent of total bond holdings, SGS exposure now exceeds central government securities (33 percent). The RBI warns that this deepens the link between state finances and bank balance sheets — meaning that if any large state faces a fiscal crisis, it could ripple directly into bank valuations. For NRIs, this is worth watching in states with stretched finances like Punjab, Kerala, or West Bengal.

**Second, long-term institutional investors — insurers and pension funds — are shifting from bonds into equities.** This leaves the government bond market more reliant on banks and foreign investors for absorption, potentially increasing yield volatility at a time when the government's borrowing needs remain elevated.

## The Global Backdrop: AI Bubbles and Sovereign Debt

The RBI's report arrived on the same day the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) published its own annual assessment, and the tone was markedly less reassuring. The BIS flagged the AI investment boom as a potential bubble — warning that intense competition, supply bottlenecks, and reliance on complex debt structures for AI infrastructure spending echo patterns seen in previous boom-and-bust cycles.

The BIS also raised alarms about record-high sovereign debt levels globally and the growing role of highly leveraged hedge funds in government bond markets, creating what it called "a new sovereign-financial stability nexus." Translation: when bond markets buckle, the shockwaves will travel further and faster than they used to.

For India, the global risks are not academic. Foreign portfolio investors bought a record $3 billion in Indian government bonds in June alone — attracted by newly removed capital gains and withholding taxes. If global risk appetite reverses, those inflows could turn into outflows quickly.

## What NRI Investors Should Take Away

The RBI's report confirms that Indian banks, as a system, are in their best shape in over a decade. For NRIs running SIPs into Indian equity mutual funds, holding FCNR deposits, or maintaining direct stock positions in Indian financials, this is genuinely encouraging.

But the risks flagged — state debt exposure, the pivot of long-term investors away from bonds, and a global environment where AI hype and sovereign debt fragilities could trigger sudden repricing — merit attention. The smart posture for NRI investors is to lean into India's structural strength while keeping an eye on the tails.

The measures India has taken in June — scrapping capital gains taxes on foreign bond investments, extending subsidized forex swap facilities for banks, and broadening the eligible securities pool for foreign investment — are designed to lock in exactly this window of opportunity. Whether the window stays open depends on forces well beyond Mumbai's control.

*The RBI's Financial Stability Report was released on June 30, 2026. The full report is available on the RBI's website.*
